pos: n. (royal capital and university city of Poland, English Cracow; the first centre of Polish evangelical religion)
etymology: From Polish Krakow, the town of Krak; Latin Cracovia, English formerly Cracow.
biblical_def: Krakow was the royal seat, the university and the first Polish city in which evangelical doctrine was openly discussed. Its printers issued Lutheran books in the 1520s in defiance of edicts; its university sheltered the humanists who read the new theology; and the court of Sigismund Augustus was full of men who corresponded with Calvin, Bullinger and Melanchthon, so that for a quarter of a century it looked as though the Polish crown might go over. It did not. The king died in 1572 without settling the matter, the Jesuits made Krakow their Polish headquarters, and within two generations the Commonwealth was Catholic again. The dictionary records Krakow because its history is the record of a church whose hope was in the court. The gospel does reach kings and ought to be carried to them — “ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake” (Mat 10:18) — and a king who almost persuades is still not persuaded.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a king as the sovereign of a nation, a monarch; a governor as one invested with supreme authority; and diligent as steady in application to business.
webster_full: KING, n. The sovereign of a nation; a monarch.
GOVERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority; the steward of a household.
DILIGENT, a. Steady in application to business; constant in effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
PRINCE, n. The chief of a body of men; the ruler of a tribe or people.
scriptures: And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles.
Act 9:15
But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel:
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.
corruption_summary: Poland's royal capital, where evangelical religion nearly won the crown and the Jesuits later made their headquarters.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the strategy of winning a nation by winning its elite, which is attractive because it looks efficient and which failed completely in Poland. The Reformed had the court, the nobility and the printers; they had comparatively little of the peasantry, and when the court turned, nothing held.

The principle to recover is that rulers are to be preached to and never relied on. The commission expects it: “ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles” (Mat 10:18). Paul is appointed to it specifically: “he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings” (Act 9:15). A competent man will find himself in such company: “he shall stand before kings” (Pro 22:29). And the result is often Agrippa's: “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian” (Act 26:28).

“to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings” (Act 9:15) — a court corresponding with Calvin and Bullinger.
“Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian” (Act 26:28) — Sigismund Augustus dead in 1572, nothing settled.

pos: n. (Polish town; the Reformed school called the Sarmatian Athens, and the cradle of Polish antitrinitarianism)
etymology: From Polish Pinczow, from a personal name Pinko; Latin Pinczovia.
biblical_def: Pinczow was the headquarters of the Polish Reformed church and the place where it split. Under the Olesnicki family the town held the Reformed synods of the 1550s, a school so good that its admirers called it the Sarmatian Athens, and the translation team that produced the Brest Bible. It is also where the antitrinitarian trouble began: Peter Gonesius came to the synod of 1556 denying the eternal deity of the Son, the Italians Blandrata and Stancaro pressed the question further, and by 1565 the Polish church had divided into the Major Church, Reformed and Trinitarian, and the Minor Church, which became Socinian. The dictionary records Pinczow because the gravest heresies in church history have usually come out of the best schools, from men already inside. “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heresy as a fundamental error in religion or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine, a heretic as one who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the faith, and to try as to examine and prove by a test.
webster_full: HERESY, n. [Gr. to take, a choosing.] A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
HERETIC, n. A person under any religion, but particularly the christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.
TRY, v.t. [Fr. trier, to pick out, to sift.] To examine; to make experiment on; to prove by a test.
ACAD'EMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university or college, and a common school.
scriptures: Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
corruption_summary: The Polish Reformed headquarters and school, and where antitrinitarianism divided the church between 1556 and 1565.
corruption_paragraphs: Socinianism is the live corruption, and it did not die with the Minor Church. Its two central denials — that the Son is of one substance with the Father from eternity, and that His death was a penal satisfaction for sin — survive wherever Christ is honoured as teacher and example and not confessed as God, which includes a great deal of liberal Protestantism and most modern unitarian religion.

The principle to recover is that heresy arises from within and must be tried, named and refused. Paul warns the elders of Ephesus about their own number: “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30). Discernment is commanded of the whole church: “try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jo 4:1). The mechanism is named as quiet introduction: false teachers “privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them” (2Pe 2:1). And the procedure ends in rejection after warning: “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10).

pos: n. (Polish town, German Lissa; refuge of the exiled Bohemian Brethren and Comenius's school)
etymology: From Polish Leszno, from leszczyna, a hazel wood; German Lissa.
biblical_def: Leszno was where the Bohemian Brethren went when Bohemia was closed to them. The Leszczynski family, Protestant magnates, settled the exiles on their lands from 1628, and the town became the Unity's headquarters in exile for thirty years: its gymnasium was reckoned among the best in Poland, John Amos Comenius taught and then led it, and the works that made his name — the Janua Linguarum Reserata among them — were written there. In 1656, in the Swedish war, Polish troops burned the town for its Protestantism and Comenius lost his library and manuscripts for the second time in his life. He went to Amsterdam and died there. The dictionary records Leszno because the Brethren built a school in a borrowed country and taught the world from it, which is what Scripture means by sojourning in faith. “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country” (Heb 11:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to sojourn as to dwell in a place as a temporary resident, a pilgrim as one that travels to a distance from his own country, and a tabernacle as a tent, a temporary habitation.
webster_full: SOJOURN, v.i. To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident.
PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveller; particularly, one that travels to a distance from his own country.
TABERNACLE, n. A tent; a temporary habitation; in Scripture, the movable house of God in the wilderness.
SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, or any branch of learning.
scriptures: Heb 11:9
By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Gen 47:9

And Jacob said unto Pharaoh, The days of the years of my pilgrimage are an hundred and thirty years: few and evil have the days of the years of my life been, and have not attained unto the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their pilgrimage.
For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers: our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is none abiding.
corruption_summary: The exiled Brethren's headquarters from 1628 and Comenius's school, burned by Polish troops in 1656.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the instinct of a displaced church to live provisionally — to put off building, teaching and publishing until it has a settled home. The Brethren at Leszno built the best school in the country on land they did not own, in a country not their own, and lost it, and the books outlived the building.

The principle to recover is that faith builds in a strange country, knowing it is a strange country. Abraham's pattern is given: “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles” (Heb 11:9). The patriarchs died without receiving what was promised and said so: they “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13). Jacob called his whole life by that name: “The days of the years of my pilgrimage are an hundred and thirty years” (Gen 47:9). And David prayed it over the richest moment of his reign: “For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers” (1Ch 29:15).

roots_lines: Greek paroikeo (G3939) — to dwell beside, to sojourn; Hebrews 11:9.
Greek skene (G4633) — a tent, a tabernacle; Hebrews 11:9.

“For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners” (1Ch 29:15) — the town burned in 1656, his library lost twice.

pos: n. (capital of Lithuania, Polish Wilno; the Reformed church under the Radziwill patronage)
etymology: From Lithuanian Vilnius, from the river Vilnia; Polish Wilno.
biblical_def: Vilnius was the capital of the Grand Duchy and the seat of Lithuanian Protestantism, and its whole position depended on one family. Nicholas Radziwill the Black, chancellor of Lithuania, went over to the Reformed in 1553, turned the Catholic churches of his towns into Reformed ones, paid for the Brest Bible, and made the Evangelical Reformed church in Vilnius the largest congregation in the city. His own son returned to Rome, the Jesuits opened a college that became the university, and in 1639 a riot drove the Reformed congregation outside the city walls, where it stayed. The dictionary records Vilnius because a church resting on a patron falls with him. “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3) is a verse about exactly this, and Lithuania is its illustration.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prince as the chief of a body of men, the ruler of a tribe or people; confidence as a trusting or reliance, an assurance of mind in the integrity of another; and to trust as to place confidence in, to rely on.
webster_full: PRINCE, n. The chief of a body of men; the ruler of a tribe or people.
CONFIDENCE, n. [L. confidentia, from confido; con and fido, to trust.] A trusting or reliance; an assurance of mind or firm belief in the integrity, stability or veracity of another.
TRUST, v.t. To place confidence in; to rely on.
PA'TRON, n. A protector; one who countenances or supports; a defender.
scriptures: Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes.
Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
Isa 2:22
Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?
corruption_summary: The Radziwill patronage made the Reformed church of Vilnius the city's largest, and his heirs' return to Rome unmade it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern equivalent of magnate patronage: a congregation or a ministry built on one donor, one gifted man, or one political alignment, which looks like strength while the support holds and leaves nothing behind when it is withdrawn.

The principle to recover is that confidence placed in men is forbidden and confidence in the LORD is commanded, and the difference is not a matter of degree. The psalm states the prohibition with its reason: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3). The comparison is drawn plainly: “It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes” (Psa 118:9). Jeremiah puts it under a curse: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5). And Isaiah gives the measure of the man relied on: “Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isa 2:22).

Hebrew nadib (H5081) — a noble, a willing prince; Psalm 146:3.

“It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes” (Psa 118:9) — his son returned to Rome.
“Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isa 2:22) — the congregation driven outside the walls, 1639.

pos: n. (town of the Grand Duchy, Polish Brzesc Litewski; where the Brest Bible was printed in 1563)
etymology: From Slavic Berestye, the place of elms, with Litovsk, of Lithuania.
biblical_def: Brest-Litovsk gave Poland its first complete Bible translated from the original tongues. Nicholas Radziwill paid for it, a team of Polish and foreign scholars worked on it for six years at Pinczow and Brest, and the folio appeared in 1563 — called the Brest Bible or the Radziwill Bible, with the Old Testament from the Hebrew and the New from the Greek. Within a few years the patron's son was buying up and burning the copies his father had paid for. The same town gave its name, in 1596, to the Union of Brest, by which much of the Ruthenian Orthodox hierarchy submitted to Rome while keeping its rite. The dictionary records Brest for the Bible. A translation from the originals is the whole counsel of God put into a nation's hands, and nothing may be added to it or taken from it: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a version as a translation rendered from another language, to diminish as to lessen or make less by any means, and a shield as a broad piece of defensive armour.
webster_full: VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
DIMINISH, v.t. To lessen; to make less or smaller, by any means; opposed to increase and augment.
SHIELD, n. A broad piece of defensive armor; a buckler; used in war for the defense of the body.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct.
scriptures: Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Pro 30:5
Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
Mat 4:4
But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
corruption_summary: Where the Brest Bible of 1563, the first Polish Bible from the original tongues, was printed; and the Union of Brest, 1596.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is selective preaching, which diminishes the word not by deleting verses but by never reaching them — the doctrines of election, judgment, hell and the ordering of the sexes being the usual omissions. A nation may have a complete Bible on the shelf and hear an abridged one from the pulpit.

The principle to recover is that the whole word is given and the whole of it is to be delivered. The prohibition is two-sided: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2). Paul's defence of his ministry rests on completeness: “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27). Every part of it is tested and sound: “Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him” (Pro 30:5). And man lives by the whole of it: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” (Mat 4:4).

pos: n. (Polish town; capital of the Socinian Minor Church, with its academy and press, suppressed in 1638)
etymology: From Polish Rakow, perhaps from rak, a crayfish, the founder's arms; Latin Racovia.
biblical_def: Rakow was founded in 1569 as a refuge for the Minor Church, the wing of the Polish Reformation that had abandoned the doctrine of the Trinity, and it became the capital of European antitrinitarianism. Its press issued the Racovian Catechism of 1605, dedicated to James I of England, which denied the eternal deity of Christ, the satisfaction of divine justice by His death, and original sin as the Reformed understood it; its academy drew students from across the continent. In 1638 the Polish Diet closed the school and the press and razed the town after an incident in which students were accused of desecrating a crucifix, and in 1658 the Socinians were banished from Poland altogether. The dictionary records Rakow in order to name the error flatly. Thomas settled the question when he addressed the risen Christ: “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Socinianism as the tenets or doctrines of Socinus, who denied the divinity of Christ; the Trinity as the union of three persons in one Godhead; and Saviour as properly applied only to Jesus Christ the Redeemer.
webster_full: SOCIN'IANISM, n. The tenets or doctrines of Socinus, who denied the divinity of Christ.
TRIN'ITY, n. The union of three persons in one Godhead.
SAVIOUR, n. One that saves or preserves; but properly applied only to Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, who has opened the way to everlasting salvation by his obedience and death.
HERESY, n. [Gr. to take, a choosing.] A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;

And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.
corruption_summary: Capital of the Socinian Minor Church, home of the Racovian Catechism of 1605, razed by the Diet in 1638.
corruption_paragraphs: Socinianism is the corruption this entry exists to name, and it is the parent of modern unitarianism and of a great deal of liberal Christianity that does not use the name. Its method is to begin with what reason can accept and to adjust the text accordingly: the deity of the Son, the penal satisfaction, original sin and eternal punishment all go, and what remains is a teacher of ethics with an exemplary death.

The principle to recover is that the Son is God, of one substance with the Father, from eternity. John opens his Gospel with it and leaves no room: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1). Thomas addresses Him in those terms and is commended, not corrected: “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28). Paul names Him with the title directly: “the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13). And John closes his epistle with the same identification: “This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jo 5:20).

Greek epiphaneia (G1932) — appearing, manifestation; Titus 2:13.
Greek alethinos (G228) — true, genuine, real; 1 John 5:20.

“My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28) — the Racovian Catechism of 1605.
“This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jo 5:20) — the town razed in 1638, the Socinians banished in 1658.

pos: n. (Baltic port of royal Prussia, Polish Gdansk; reformed after the suppressed revolt of 1525)
etymology: From Polish Gdansk, of Slavic origin; German Danzig.
biblical_def: Danzig was the richest city of the Polish crown and its Reformation came by riot first and by law second. In January 1525 the guilds and the evangelical preachers overthrew the city council, abolished the mass and set up a new government; in April 1526 King Sigismund arrived with an army, executed the ringleaders, restored the old order and banned evangelical preaching for a generation. The city reformed anyway, gradually and legally, and by the 1550s was granted the Augsburg Confession by royal privilege; it later carried a substantial Reformed minority alongside the Lutheran majority. The dictionary records Danzig because the contrast between 1525 and 1557 is instructive: what the rising lost in a year the ordinary processes of a city gained and kept for three centuries. “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ordinance as a rule established by authority, a permanent rule of action; sedition as a factious commotion of the people rising in opposition to law; and subject as placed or situate under.
webster_full: ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action.
SEDITION, n. A factious commotion of the people; a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law.
SUBJECT, a. — Placed or situate under.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
scriptures: Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;
Rom 13:2
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.
Tit 3:1
Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work,
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:
corruption_summary: The 1525 evangelical revolt crushed by Sigismund in 1526, and the lawful reformation that followed and lasted.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a righteous cause licenses revolutionary means, which has wrecked more reformations than persecution has. Danzig's guildsmen were right about the mass and wrong about the method, and their rising set the city back thirty years.

The principle to recover is that submission to lawful authority is required of Christians and is not suspended by the authority's errors in religion. The command is comprehensive: “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme” (1Pe 2:13). Resistance to the office is named as resistance to God: “Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God” (Rom 13:2). The duty is to be taught and remembered: “Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates” (Tit 3:1). And the proverb warns against the company of the restless: “meddle not with them that are given to change” (Pro 24:21).

Greek ktisis (G2937) — a thing instituted, an ordinance; 1 Peter 2:13.
Greek antitassomai (G498) — to set oneself against, to resist; Romans 13:2.
Greek diatage (G1296) — an ordinance, a disposition appointed; Romans 13:2.
Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Titus 3:1.
usage: “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13) — the guild rising of January 1525.
“resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God” (Rom 13:2) — Sigismund's army and the executions of 1526.
“meddle not with them that are given to change” (Pro 24:21) — and the Augsburg Confession by royal privilege.

pos: n. (Prussian city of the Polish crown, German Thorn; host of the Colloquium Charitativum of 1645)
etymology: From Polish Torun, from the Teutonic castle of Thoron; German Thorn.
biblical_def: Torun hosted the most serious attempt at religious reconciliation in seventeenth-century Europe. King Wladyslaw IV summoned Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed theologians to a Colloquium Charitativum in the city in 1645, with Comenius among those consulted; it sat for a month, produced an exchange of papers and no agreement, and dispersed. Seventy-nine years later the same city saw the Tumult of Thorn, in which a Protestant crowd and a Jesuit procession collided, and the Polish courts executed the burgomaster and nine citizens, an act that shocked Protestant Europe. The dictionary records Torun because the two events together draw the line it holds: Christians may meet, state their differences honestly, and part; they may not yoke what Scripture has separated. “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a yoke as a piece of timber fitted to the necks of oxen and so a mark of servitude; to separate as to disunite, to set apart for a particular use; and darkness as, figuratively, ignorance or sin.
webster_full: YOKE, n. A piece of timber fitted to the necks of oxen; a mark of servitude; slavery; bondage.
SEPARATE, v.t. To disunite; to divide; to set apart for a particular purpose or use.
DARKNESS, n. Absence of light; figuratively, ignorance, sin, or spiritual blindness.
SYNCRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance.
scriptures: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Eph 5:11
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.
If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed:
corruption_summary: The Colloquium Charitativum of 1645, which produced papers and no agreement, and the Tumult of Thorn in 1724.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is the ecumenism that treats institutional union as a good in itself, so that the terms of agreement are adjusted downward until a document can be signed. Torun did not do that — it stated the differences and dispersed — and that is the model the dictionary commends: honest conference without false union.

The principle to recover is that fellowship in worship and mission requires agreement in the faith, and that separation is commanded where it is lacking. Paul forbids the unequal yoke and gives the reason as a question: “what communion hath light with darkness?” (2Co 6:14). The command follows: “come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing” (2Co 6:17). The believer's duty toward error is exposure, not partnership: “have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11). And John forbids even the courtesy that would imply endorsement: “If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house” (2Jo 1:10).
roots_summary: Greek heterozugeo (G2086), to be unequally yoked; Greek aphorizo (G873), to separate.
roots_lines: Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be yoked with a different kind; 2 Corinthians 6:14.
Greek metoche (G3352) — a sharing, a partnership; 2 Corinthians 6:14.
Greek aphorizo (G873) — to mark off, to separate; 2 Corinthians 6:17.
Greek sugkoinoneo (G4790) — to have fellowship with, to partake; Ephesians 5:11.
Greek elencho (G1651) — to reprove, to expose; Ephesians 5:11.
usage: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14) — the Colloquium Charitativum, 1645.
“come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — papers exchanged and no agreement reached.
“rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11) — and the Tumult of Thorn, 1724.

pos: n. (Polish village; site of the first general synod of the Polish Reformed churches, 1556)
etymology: From Polish Secemin, from a personal name; Latin Seceminium.
biblical_def: Secemin is a village in Little Poland where, in January 1556, the scattered evangelical congregations of the region held their first general synod and began to be a church rather than a collection of patrons' chapels. They agreed on a confession, provided for the calling and examination of ministers, and appointed superintendents; the same meeting heard Peter Gonesius deny the eternal deity of the Son and referred the matter, which began the long antitrinitarian crisis. The dictionary records Secemin because organisation is not a declension from spiritual vitality but its ordinary preservative, and because the apostolic churches were organised in exactly this way as soon as they existed. “And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord” (Act 14:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion, to ordain as to establish, institute or appoint, and fasting as abstinence from food, especially in token of religious humiliation.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. In church history, a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
ORDAIN, v.t. [L. ordino, from ordo, order.] To set; to establish; to institute; to constitute; to appoint.
FASTING, n. Abstinence from food; the act of abstaining from food, especially in token of religious humiliation.
PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of all the pastors of churches within a certain district.
scriptures: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Which also they did, and sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
Act 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
corruption_summary: The first general synod of the Polish Reformed churches, January 1556, which also first heard the antitrinitarian denial.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the romance of the unstructured church, which treats constitutions, examinations and courts as a later accretion on a simpler original. The original had all of them within twenty years of Pentecost, and the Polish churches that did not organise were absorbed by whichever magnate owned the village.

The principle to recover is that Christ's churches are to have ordained officers, appointed by the laying on of hands after examination, with prayer. The pattern is apostolic and immediate: “when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord” (Act 14:23). Elders are a body able to receive and administer: the relief was sent “to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul” (Act 11:30). Ordination is by a presbytery: “with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14). And officers are chosen on examined character: “look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3).
roots_summary: Greek cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint by stretching out the hand; Greek presbuterion (G4244), a body of elders.
roots_lines: Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint, to ordain by vote or hand; Acts 14:23.
Greek nesteia (G3521) — fasting, abstinence in humiliation; Acts 14:23.
Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to commit, to commend to another; Acts 14:23.
Greek presbuterion (G4244) — a presbytery, a body of elders; 1 Timothy 4:14.
Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness, of honest report; Acts 6:3.
usage: “when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the synod of January 1556.
“with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14) — a confession agreed and superintendents appointed.
“seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3) — and Gonesius's denial referred.

pos: n. (Polish city; the Union of 1569 that joined Poland and Lithuania, and a Reformed and antitrinitarian centre)
etymology: From Polish Lublin, from a personal name Lubla; Latin Lublinum.
biblical_def: Lublin was where the Polish Diet sat in 1569 and bound the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into one Commonwealth with one parliament, one coinage and one foreign policy. Lublin was also a religious crossroads: a Reformed congregation under noble patronage, an antitrinitarian congregation that made the city one of the Minor Church's main centres, a large and ancient Jewish community with a famous yeshiva, and the Catholic establishment, all within one set of walls. The dictionary records the city because the union of two peoples by statute is an instructive contrast with the union Scripture describes: the Commonwealth's union was political and lasted two centuries, and the union of men in Christ is older than nations and outlasts them. “he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines partition as the act of dividing or the state of being divided, a nation as a body of people united under one government, and peace as a state of quiet and freedom from disturbance.
webster_full: PARTITION, n. The act of dividing, or state of being divided.
NATION, n. A body of people inhabiting the same country, united under one government.
PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation.
U'NION, n. [L. unio, to unite, from unus, one.]
scriptures: Eph 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Col 3:11
Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all.
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: The Union of 1569 joining Poland and Lithuania, in a city holding Reformed, antitrinitarian, Jewish and Catholic communities at once.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the use of these texts to abolish the distinctions God Himself made. Galatians 3:28 says that Jew and Greek, bond and free, male and female are one in Christ as to justification and standing before God; it does not dissolve the creational difference of the sexes or the order of headship and submission in household and church, which the same apostle teaches in the same letters. The dictionary names that reading as a corruption and holds the text's own sense.

The principle to recover is that Christ Himself is the union of His people, and that it is achieved by the removal of enmity rather than by the levelling of creation. The wall is named and so is the one who removed it: “he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14). The oneness is located precisely: “ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:28). What is put off is the old man with his divisions: “but Christ is all, and in all” (Col 3:11). And the common origin of all nations is a fact of creation and providence: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Act 17:26).
roots_summary: Greek mesotoichon (G3320), a middle wall; Greek eirene (G1515), peace.
roots_lines: Greek mesotoichon (G3320) — a middle wall, a dividing partition; Ephesians 2:14.
Greek phragmos (G5418) — a fence, a hedge of separation; Ephesians 2:14.
Greek eirene (G1515) — peace, reconciliation effected; Ephesians 2:14.
Greek heis (G1520) — one, a single whole; Galatians 3:28.
Greek horothesia (G3734) — a fixed boundary, an appointed limit; Acts 17:26.
usage: “he is our peace, who hath made both one” (Eph 2:14) — the Union of Lublin, 1569.
“ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:28) — Reformed, antitrinitarian, Jewish and Catholic within one wall.
“hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26) — one parliament, one coinage, two peoples.
